abstract: Dr. Calvert's lecture covers the gynecologic exam in menopausal women, including proper speculum and bimanual technique, anatomy of the uterus and ovaries, and the evaluation and management of vaginal atrophy. He emphasizes understanding pelvic anatomy to improve exam accuracy and discusses the natural history of vasomotor symptoms, the role of hormone therapy, and a stepwise protocol for treating vaginal atrophy with topical estradiol.
key_points: The Bartholin glands are located near the introitus, not the clitoris, and should not be palpable normally.
When placing a speculum, aim for the posterior fornix to entrap the cervix between the blades.
The uterus is suspended by the broad ligament and should move freely in all directions; restricted movement suggests adhesions or pathology.
Ovaries are palpable about 60% of the time; if felt, they should slide like a marble between the fingers and be mobile.
A retroverted or retroflexed uterus may require a rectovaginal exam to palpate the fundus, especially before endometrial biopsy.
Vasomotor symptoms resolve spontaneously in about 80% of women over time, even without treatment.
Hormone replacement therapy is not indicated for perimenopausal symptoms; birth control pills are used instead to control ovarian function.
Vaginal atrophy is the most common cause of postcoital spotting in menopausal women, accounting for about 80% of cases.
Topical estradiol (not conjugated estrogen) is preferred for treating vaginal atrophy; treatment requires months of gradual dose reduction.
The goal of atrophy treatment is to normalize the vaginal epithelium using the lowest effective maintenance dose, typically 1 gram once or twice weekly.
Topical estrogen for atrophic vaginitis requires consistent use over weeks to months for full healing, not just symptom relief.
Patients may worsen if estrogen is stopped too soon or dose is reduced too quickly.
